title: I am the bread of life (John 6:35)
word: I am the bread of life
hook: the first great I am: whoever comes to me shall not hunger

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pool with five porches, and a question: wilt thou be made whole? What was your honest answer? Day five hundred three.

The day before, on a hillside by the Sea of Galilee, five thousand men sat down on the grass and ate from five barley loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. That night the crowd wanted to make him king. He slipped away. Now, the next morning, they've crossed the lake in boats to find him again. And he tells them, plainly: you're looking for me not because you saw signs, but because you ate the bread and were filled. They want more breakfast. He's about to offer them something else.
screen: `FIVE THOUSAND FED ON A HILLSIDE.` → `THEY WANT TO MAKE HIM KING.` → `THEY COME BACK FOR MORE BREAD.`

segments.voice: The crowd pushes back. What sign will you give us? Our fathers ate manna in the desert; Moses gave them bread from heaven. It's a fair challenge. Yesterday's loaves were impressive, but manna fed a whole people for forty years. Jesus corrects them gently: it wasn't Moses who gave the bread, it's my Father who gives the true bread from heaven. And they say, almost like the woman at the well: Lord, give us always this bread. Then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall not hunger: and he that believeth in me shall never thirst." This is the first of seven great sayings in John's Gospel that begin I am and then name a picture. I am the bread of life. The light of the world. The door. The good shepherd. The resurrection and the life. The way, the truth and the life. The true vine. We'll meet most of them in the weeks ahead. Each takes something ordinary and says: this is what I am to you. Bread is the most ordinary of all. Not a feast. Not a delicacy. The thing on every table, the thing you need every single day. Not hunger, not thirst: he's not promising they'll never miss a meal. He's speaking of a deeper hunger, the one that comes back no matter how much we eat. Catholics hear this whole chapter as pointing toward the Eucharist, and we'll go further into that tomorrow. Today, stay with the plain image. Bread is daily. The promise is daily too.
screen: `OUR FATHERS ATE MANNA.` · `LORD, GIVE US ALWAYS THIS BREAD.` · `THE FIRST OF SEVEN I AMS.` · `BREAD: ORDINARY AND DAILY.` · then, large: `I AM THE BREAD OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray before eating. Think of your next meal, or if food is nearby, set it in front of you. Settle, and breathe. Before the first bite, stop. Look at it. Think of the hands that grew it, carried it, cooked it. Many Catholic families say a short grace before meals, often the old one that begins bless us, O Lord. If you pray, you can say it, or simply give thanks in your own words. If you don't, just pause and let the food be noticed before it's eaten. The bell holds the time.
I am the bread of life. The first of John's seven I am sayings: whoever comes to him shall not hunger. Today's word.
screen: `I AM THE BREAD OF LIFE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bread of life. Today, don't eat your first bite of any meal without a pause. Day five hundred three.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice metaphor about spiritual nourishment.
what it means: Jesus offers himself as the daily bread that answers the deepest hunger, and the chapter goes on toward the Eucharist.
what a scholar hears: the first of John's seven 'I am' sayings with a predicate, set against the manna of Exodus 16.
